hero.lede: I’m Ajay Kumar. Eight years of SEO, paid, brand and growth for Web3, real estate and fashion — and the marketer who actually builds the automation most consultants only recommend. n8n workflows, lead-qualifying agents, reporting that runs itself.

thesis.label: The idea
thesis.quote: Most marketing plans don’t fail. They die in the queue of manual work behind them.
notes: The strategy is sound. Then somebody has to route the leads, chase the follow-up, pull the report and tag the campaign — by hand, every week, because nobody budgeted an engineer to automate it.

I build that layer myself. n8n workflows that move data between your ad accounts, your CRM and your CMS without anyone copying a spreadsheet, and AI agents that qualify a lead, draft a reply or flag an anomaly before a person has to look at it.
I am not a software engineer and I won’t pretend to be one. What I build is the automation layer between the plan and the result — the part most marketing consultants can only tell you that you need.

work.label: Selected work
work.title: Numbers, in context.
work.lede: One from each market. Full write-ups — including what didn’t work — on the case studies page.

cases.title: From X hype and Telegram chatter to 40,000 real holders
cases.desc: A layer-2 protocol had a loud X following and 90,000 Telegram members, with no idea which of them were real. We tied X and Telegram activity to on-chain wallets with an agent-run qualification pipeline, killed the bot-farmed airdrop tiers, and rebuilt the launch funnel around proof-of-use rather than proof-of-presence.

cases.title: Nine luxury residences, one brand worth the premium
cases.desc: Leading marketing for a luxury developer with nine live residences, we built one brand that buyers trusted to hold its price. We owned the brand identity and storytelling, invite-only launch previews and experience-centre events, high-net-worth and NRI targeting across premium media and paid channels, editorial content and SEO, a CRM-led concierge journey from first enquiry to handover, and wealth-manager and channel-partner programmes. Every booking fed back into the plan, so spend went to the buyers who mattered, not the most clicks.

cases.title: An agent that decided when to message, not a calendar
cases.desc: Strong acquisition, almost no second purchase, and a lifecycle calendar nobody trusted. We built an n8n workflow that reads what someone actually wears and returns, and an agent that decides the next message and channel — replacing a fixed send schedule with one that runs on real behaviour, unattended.

process.label: How it works
process.title: A process built to kill bad ideas early.

steps.title: Diagnose
steps.desc: Two weeks inside your analytics, ad accounts, search console and CRM. You get a written diagnosis of where growth is actually stuck — not a ninety-slide deck about your industry.

steps.title: Prioritise
steps.desc: Every opportunity scored by impact, effort and time-to-signal. We agree on the three that matter this quarter and deliberately ignore the rest.

steps.title: Ship
steps.desc: Weekly execution against a public backlog. Fixes, campaigns, pages and content go live in small batches so we learn fast and compound.

steps.title: Compound
steps.desc: Monthly review against one north-star metric. Winners get budget, losers get killed early, and the playbook gets written down for your team.

items.q: How technical are you, exactly?
items.a: I don’t write production software, and I’ll tell you that before you have to ask. What I do build, myself, is the automation layer: n8n workflows that connect your ad accounts, CRM and CMS, and AI agents that qualify leads, draft replies or flag anomalies without a human in the loop. I’m also fluent enough in your stack to hold a real conversation with your engineers when something needs to sit deeper in the product.

items.q: Why does automation matter when hiring a marketer?
items.a: Because most marketing budget is spent on work a workflow could do for free. Routing leads, pulling reports, tagging campaigns, chasing follow-up — a marketer who cannot automate that will spend your retainer doing it by hand, or won’t notice it’s costing you at all.

items.q: Do you only work with Web3, real estate and fashion companies?
items.a: Those are where most of the last eight years went, and they are useful range: one technical market, one data-and-CRM market, one platform-and-creative market. I take work outside them when the shape of the problem is familiar. If your category is genuinely unlike anything I have touched, I will say so on the first call rather than bill you for my learning curve.

items.q: Do you work as a consultant or run campaigns hands-on?
items.a: Both, depending on what you need. Some clients want a fractional head of growth who sets strategy and manages an in-house team; others want me executing SEO and paid campaigns directly. Most engagements open with a diagnosis sprint and then move into retained execution.

items.q: How long before we see results?
items.a: Paid media usually shows signal in two to four weeks. Conversion work compounds from the first shipped test. SEO is slower and more honest: meaningful movement in three to four months, compounding returns from month six. If your timeline and your channel choice do not match, I will say so before we start.

items.q: What does an engagement cost?
items.a: Engagements are scoped by outcome, not by hours. A diagnosis sprint, a monthly retainer and a fractional growth-lead arrangement are the three common shapes. We agree the scope and the number on the first call, before there is a proposal.

items.q: Do you work with clients outside India?
items.a: Yes. Roughly half of the work is with teams in the US, UK, UAE and Singapore, all remote — Web3 especially tends to be distributed by default. I keep a real overlap window with wherever the core team sits.

cta.label: Let’s talk
cta.title: Your next 90 days, mapped in one call.
cta.lede: Free, thirty minutes, no deck. You leave with a written view of the three highest-leverage moves for your business — whether or not we end up working together.

hero.label: Growth Marketing
hero.lede: Doubling traffic is expensive. Doubling the share of that traffic which converts, activates and stays is usually cheaper, faster and permanent.

overview.label: Overview
paras: Growth marketing is the discipline of finding where value leaks out of your funnel and fixing the biggest hole first. It is unglamorous, quantitative, and by far the best return on effort in most companies I meet.

I start by mapping the whole journey with real numbers attached — visit to signup, signup to activation, activation to paid, paid to retained — then finding the step where drop-off is worst relative to benchmark. That step gets the quarter’s attention. Everything else waits.

From there it is a disciplined experiment cadence: a documented hypothesis, a defined success metric, a sample size agreed before launch, and a written decision at the end. Winners roll out; losers get recorded so nobody re-runs them in eighteen months.

approach.label: Approach
approach.title: How I think about growth marketing.
paras: Find the constraint, then be boring about it. Most teams run experiments everywhere at once and change nothing meaningfully. One well-chosen bottleneck, worked for a quarter, beats twenty scattered tests.

I am strict about statistics because the alternative is expensive superstition. A test needs its sample size agreed before launch and a pre-registered success metric, or it becomes a story we tell ourselves about a 4% lift that was noise.

And retention beats acquisition in almost every model. A ten percent improvement in month-two retention changes what you can afford to pay for a customer, which changes every channel decision downstream — which is why the fashion lifecycle work usually pays for itself faster than any ad optimisation would have.

items.q: What’s the difference between growth marketing and regular marketing?
items.a: Scope and method. Traditional marketing usually owns acquisition; growth marketing owns the whole funnel through to retention and revenue, and works through structured experiments with a stated hypothesis rather than an annual plan.

items.q: Do we need a lot of traffic for CRO to work?
items.a: For statistically valid A/B testing, yes — roughly a few thousand relevant sessions a month per variant. Below that, qualitative research, user testing and evidence-based rewrites deliver more than underpowered tests that never reach significance.

items.q: Can you work with our product and engineering teams?
items.a: Yes, and the best results come from it. I write specs engineers can implement, respect the roadmap, and prioritise by effort as well as impact so growth work doesn’t become a tax on the product team.

items.q: How do you prioritise which experiments to run?
items.a: Impact on the identified constraint, effort to implement, and time to a readable signal. Anything that doesn’t touch the current bottleneck goes in the backlog with a date, not into this quarter.

approach.label: Approach
approach.title: How I think about automation.
paras: Automate the queue, not the judgment. The work worth automating is repetitive and well-defined — routing, tagging, reporting, first-pass replies. The work that stays human is the 20% that actually requires taste or accountability. Getting that boundary wrong is how a company ends up with a chatbot promising refunds it can’t authorise.

I build in n8n because it’s transparent — you can open any workflow and see exactly what it does, unlike a black-box SaaS automation tool you’re renting by the seat. Every workflow I hand over comes documented well enough that your team can extend it without me.

Across three markets, this looks different every time: a Web3 team needs an agent watching on-chain events, a real estate developer needs leads routed to the right project and salesperson in under a minute, a fashion brand needs post-purchase flows triggered by what someone actually wears rather than a fixed day count.

items.q: Do I need to already use n8n?
items.a: No. Most clients don’t have any automation in place, which is normal — I set up the account, build the workflows and document them so your team can read and extend them later.

items.q: What happens if the AI agent gets something wrong?
items.a: It’s designed to. Every agent has a defined confidence boundary: below it, the item goes to a human instead of guessing. We set that boundary deliberately, and it’s the first thing we tune once real data comes in.

items.q: Is this the same as buying a chatbot tool?
items.a: No. Off-the-shelf tools rent you a narrow, closed workflow. n8n workflows are built around your actual stack and your actual rules, you own the account, and there’s no vendor lock-in if you want to move it in-house later.

items.q: Can this replace a marketing hire?
items.a: No, and I won’t pitch it that way. It removes the repetitive load so the person in the seat spends their time on strategy and judgment instead of copying data between tools.

items.a: The brands I’ve worked with are listed on the home and about pages, but the specific numbers and tactics behind each case study sit under NDA or involve competitive strategy the client would rather not publish — particularly in Web3, where launch mechanics are the moat. On a call I can walk you through the accounts, dashboards and specific decisions, including references from clients happy to speak.

items.q: Are these results typical?
items.a: No result is typical — that’s the honest answer. These are engagements that went well, chosen because they show the method. I’ve also had campaigns that failed, and I’ll happily tell you about those on a call, because what went wrong is usually more instructive.

items.q: Three very different industries — doesn’t that mean shallow expertise?
items.a: Each one is technically different in a way the others could not have taught me. Web3 forced me to understand rendering and on-chain data. Real estate forced me to understand CRM and attribution across a twelve-month cycle. Fashion forced me to understand feeds, platforms and creative velocity. The vocabulary changes every time; the diagnosis does not.

items.q: Can I speak to a past client?
items.a: Yes. Once we’re past a first conversation and there’s a real fit, I’ll connect you with clients at a comparable stage and in a comparable market.

profile.label: Profile
paras: I’m Ajay Kumar — a marketing consultant who spends about as much time in Search Console, GA4 and a staging environment as in a brand deck.

I started in content and SEO, moved into performance marketing for real estate developers, led growth at a Web3 company through a full market cycle, and picked up fashion clients along the way because a friend’s label was discounting itself to death and I thought I could see why.

Somewhere in there I stopped waiting on other people to automate the boring parts and started building it myself. n8n is where most of it lives now — workflows that move leads between an ad account and a CRM, agents that qualify or route them before a human sees them, reporting that assembles itself instead of eating a Monday morning. I’m not a software engineer and I don’t write production code, but I ship automation that used to sit on somebody’s to-do list indefinitely. Across three markets that are technically nothing alike, that has been the most useful thing about me.

These days I work with four to six clients at a time, as either a fractional growth lead or a strategist embedded with an in-house team. I care about compounding assets over rented attention, about telling clients the uncomfortable thing early, and about leaving behind a team that no longer needs me.

Moved into performance marketing for real estate developers. Long consideration cycles, expensive leads, and a CRM that finally taught me the difference between a lead and a buyer.

principles.label: How I work
principles.title: Four things I won’t compromise on.

items.title: Measure it or don’t ship it
items.desc: If we can’t define what success looks like before launch, we aren’t running a campaign, we’re decorating. Every initiative gets a metric and a date attached upfront.

items.title: No dark patterns, ever
items.desc: No fake urgency, no bought links, no inflated case-study numbers, no growth tactic I’d be embarrassed to explain to your customers. Short-term tricks become long-term liabilities — a lesson Web3 teaches faster than most.

items.title: Say the hard thing early
items.desc: If your offer is the problem, your pricing is wrong, or the channel you asked for is a bad fit, you’ll hear it in week two — not in month six when the retainer is up for renewal.

items.q: Are you a freelancer or an agency?
items.a: Independent consultant. You work with me directly — no account manager, no junior running your campaigns while a senior name sits on the pitch deck. For specialist production I bring in a small trusted bench, and I tell you when I do.

items.q: How many clients do you take on?
items.a: Four to six at a time, depending on engagement depth. That cap is the point: it is what makes senior attention possible rather than theoretical.

items.q: Where are you based and which timezones do you cover?
items.a: India, working remotely with teams across IST, GST, GMT and US timezones. Web3 clients are distributed by default, so overlapping hours are normal rather than an accommodation.

items.q: What if my industry isn’t Web3, real estate or fashion?
items.a: Then we talk about whether the shape of your problem is familiar even if the category isn’t. Subscription economics, long consideration cycles, community-led growth and taste-driven purchases cover a lot of ground. If it’s genuinely outside what I know, I’ll say so — the first month of learning your market shouldn’t be billed to you as strategy.

items.q: Are you a developer?
items.a: No, and I say so before anyone has to ask. I don’t build your product or your app. What I do build is the automation layer around your marketing — n8n workflows and AI agents — and I’m fluent enough in how a stack works to hold a real conversation with your engineers when something needs to sit deeper in the product. If a job genuinely needs a software engineer, I will tell you that rather than quietly doing it badly.
